sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body: 94. Whoever, by secretly burying or otherwise disposing of the dead body of a child whether such child die before or after or during its birth, intentionally conceals or endeavours to conceal the birth of such child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both

learningObjectives: Master the elements of intentionally concealing the birth of a child by secret disposal of its dead body under BNS s. 94.
Understand that liability attaches whether the child died before, during, or after birth.
Analyze the requirement of secret burial or clandestine disposal aimed at preventing discovery of birth.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 94 penalizes whoever, by secretly burying or otherwise disposing of the dead body of a child whether such child die before or after or during its birth, intentionally conceals or endeavours to conceal the birth of such child, punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Criminalizes the clandestine disposal of a dead infant's body intended to conceal the fact of birth, safeguarding vital registration and preventing the concealment of infanticide.
statutoryFramework: Chapter V — Of Offences against Women and Children, BNS s. 94 (corresponding to IPC s. 318).
Actus reus: Secretly burying or otherwise disposing of the dead body of a child.
Scope: Applies whether the child died before, during, or after birth.
Mens rea: Intentionally concealing or endeavouring to conceal the birth of such child.
Punishment: Imprisonment of either description extending up to two years, or fine, or both.
essentialIngredients: A child died before, during, or after its birth.
There was a dead body of the child.
The accused secretly buried or otherwise disposed of the dead body.
The accused did so with the intention of concealing or endeavouring to conceal the birth of the child.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 94 addresses the secret disposal of dead infants. Historically and practically, this provision is invoked where an infant's birth is concealed to avoid social stigma or to cover up illegal abortions and infanticides. To establish liability, there must be a dead body (not a living child, and not an unformed early embryo incapable of being described as a child). The disposal must be secret—such as clandestine burial at night in a field, throwing into a well, or burning in secret. The specific intention must be to conceal the birth of the child from the authorities or the public. The provision applies regardless of whether the child was stillborn or died after birth.
examples: Teaching example (Secret burial in backyard): A woman gives birth to a stillborn child at seven months and secretly buries the body in a ditch behind her house in the middle of the night to conceal the fact that she was pregnant. She is liable under s. 94.

Teaching example (Public disposal without concealment): A parent leaves a dead infant in a public hospital morgue with identification. There is no secret disposal or intent to conceal birth; s. 94 is not attracted.
distinctions: Section 94 vs Section 93: Section 93 applies to abandoning a living child under 12; Section 94 applies to the secret disposal of the dead body of an infant.
Section 94 vs Murder (s. 103): If the accused killed the child after birth, the offence is murder; s. 94 covers the concealment of birth by disposing of the corpse.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who wrapped a deceased newborn infant in plastic and threw the body into a secluded ravine to prevent anyone in the village from knowing she had given birth is liable under s. 94.
Rule: Secretly disposing of the dead body of a child with intent to conceal its birth satisfies BNS s. 94.
Application: There was a dead body, secret disposal was carried out, and the intent was to conceal the birth.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 94.
